title: Usability Testing a Student Website Prototype
context: Two computing students report the results of their first round of user testing, and their supervisor separates the findings from the guesswork.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: Should we just talk through it in the order we tested things, or do you want the headline numbers first?

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: So — the prototype. You tested it with how many people?

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: Eight.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: Eight, but two of them were sort of us.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Meaning what, exactly?

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: Meaning they were people on our own course, and they knew what the site was for before they sat down at it.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Then you tested it with six. Write six. What task did you give them?

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: "Report a broken street light on Denby Road." We timed them from the home page.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Good task. It's specific, and it has an obvious end point. What happened?

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: Four of the six couldn't work out where to start. They looked at the home page for — I've got the figure here — an average of fifty-one seconds before clicking on anything at all.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Fifty-one seconds is an age. What were they looking for?

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: A button. Every one of them said afterwards that they were hunting for a big obvious button, and ours is a link in the menu called Submissions.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: Which is a word nobody outside the project uses.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: In hindsight, 'Submissions' was always going to mean something only to us.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: That's your finding, then, and it's a good one. What did you do about it?

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: We changed it to "Report a problem" and made it a proper button.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Did you test it again?

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Then you don't know. You have a hypothesis, which is better than what you had before, but the difference between design and guessing is the second test. Put it in the plan.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: There's an accessibility problem as well. The grey text on the white background is 3.1 to 1, and the standard is four and a half to one.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: How did you find that out?

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: A contrast checker. It flagged eleven elements.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: That is the sort of finding I like, because it isn't a matter of opinion — it either passes or it doesn't. Fix all eleven and run the checker again. That one you don't need users for.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: The form is the other thing. It has nine fields, and three of them are compulsory that really don't need to be.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: The telephone number especially. Two people stopped completely at the telephone number and wouldn't go on.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: One of them said — I wrote it down word for word — "why does a street light need my phone number?"

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: That is the best sentence in your whole report. Put it in. A quotation like that does more work than a paragraph of your own prose, because nobody can argue with it.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: I did wonder if it was a bit cheeky to quote him directly like that.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: It isn't cheeky, it's evidence. Use it.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: So we make the telephone number optional.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Make it optional, and say beside it why you are asking. People will give you a number if they are told what it's for. They will not give it to a blank box.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: On a phone, the map doesn't load at all below a certain screen width.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Does not load, or loads and can't be seen?

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: Doesn't load. It's a script error.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: That would explain why it worked fine on my laptop but not on my phone.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Then that isn't a design finding, that's a bug, and it belongs in a different list. Don't mix them. A report that puts a crash next to "the heading could be bigger" makes both of them look equally serious, and neither gets taken seriously.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: Fair point — we did lump those together without really thinking about it.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Before we get to priorities, though — did anything work well? I don't want the whole report to read like a list of failures.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: The confirmation screen, actually. Every single person understood immediately that their report had gone through.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: Nobody asked 'did that actually work?', which is apparently rare.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: It's rarer than it should be. Put that in as well, briefly — a report with nothing positive in it is as misleading as one with nothing negative.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: What should we fix first? We've only got three weeks.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: In this order: the thing that stops people finishing the task at all, then the thing that shuts people out, then the thing that merely annoys them. So the button, then the contrast, then the form. The heading sizes can wait forever.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: And the map?

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: The bug is not a fix-first question at all. A bug is fixed when it is found. That's a completely different rule.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: Do we need more participants for the second round?

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Six again is fine, but six different ones, and at least two of them should be people who don't use a computer every day. Your six were all twenty-year-olds studying computing. The people who actually report broken street lights are not.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: That's going to be much harder to recruit.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: It is. Ask at the community centre on Foxhall Street — they have helped three groups before you and they have never once said no.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: That's genuinely reassuring — I was dreading the recruitment part most.

script.speaker: Ines
script.text: Same. I'll draft the email to them today.

script.speaker: Dr Nowak
script.text: Good. Bring both rounds of findings together in one document before we meet again — the first round shouldn't disappear just because the second one exists.

script.speaker: Baz
script.text: Understood.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.question: How many participants does Dr Nowak say the students actually tested?
questions.explanation: Two of the eight were on the students' own course and already knew what the site was for, so Dr Nowak says: "Then you tested it with six. Write six."

questions.question: Why does Dr Nowak say the students cannot yet claim the new button works?
options: they have not tested it again
they changed two things at the same time
the contrast is still too low
questions.explanation: Baz admits they did not re-test. "Then you don't know... the difference between design and guessing is the second test."

questions.question: What does Dr Nowak say about the map not loading?
options: it should be fixed straight after the form is done
it should be listed as a bug rather than a design finding
it is caused by the width setting of the screen used
questions.explanation: "That isn't a design finding, that's a bug, and it belongs in a different list," because mixing the two makes both look equally serious.

questions.question: What does Dr Nowak recommend for the second round of testing?
options: using the same six participants again next time
increasing the number of participants from six to eight
including people who are less confident with computers
questions.explanation: "Six again is fine, but six different ones, and at least two of them should be people who don't use a computer every day."

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.sentence: Participants studied the home page for an average of ___ seconds before clicking
questions.explanation: Ines reads the figure out: "an average of fifty-one seconds before clicking on anything at all," which Dr Nowak calls an age.

questions.sentence: The menu link was called ___ , a word outsiders do not use
questions.explanation: "Ours is a link in the menu called Submissions," and Ines adds that it is "a word nobody outside the project uses."
"A contrast checker. It flagged eleven elements." Dr Nowak values this because it passes or fails rather than being a matter of opinion.
Baz reports, "It has nine fields, and three of them are compulsory that really don't need to be." Three is how many are wrongly compulsory.

questions.sentence: Two participants stopped at the field asking for their ___
questions.explanation: "Two people stopped completely at the telephone number and wouldn't go on," and one asked why a street light needed it.

questions.sentence: Order of repair: the button, then the contrast, then the ___
questions.explanation: Dr Nowak gives the order plainly: "the button, then the contrast, then the form. The heading sizes can wait forever."
